title: The Plan That Would Not Stay on the Screen
text:
Noor had practiced the neighborhood-history presentation until she could advance the slides without looking at the keyboard. She knew exactly when the photograph of the old ferry terminal would appear, when the map would zoom toward River Street, and when she would pause long enough for the audience to read a quotation from a shopkeeper who had worked there forty years earlier.

The presentation was scheduled for Saturday afternoon in the community center courtyard. Noor had asked twice whether the outdoor screen would be bright enough. She had packed an extension cable, a spare adapter, and printed notes in case she forgot a date. Her teacher, Mr. Han, had smiled at the growing pile of equipment. “You have prepared for everything,” he said.

“That's the idea,” Noor answered.

An hour before the event, clouds gathered over the courtyard. The organizers moved the chairs under the covered walkway, where the audience would stay dry if the rain remained light. The projector still worked, but the screen now faced a row of bright windows. Noor's carefully edited photographs looked washed out, and the smallest labels on her map nearly disappeared.

She tried changing the projector settings. Then she moved the screen. Then she asked an organizer whether they could turn off the courtyard lights, even though the lights were not causing the problem. Each adjustment made one thing slightly better and another thing worse. People began taking their seats.

Mr. Han carried a box toward her. Inside were the large printed photographs Noor had used while interviewing residents: the ferry terminal, the old market, a row of houses before the road was widened. She had considered the prints too plain for the final presentation.

“We could pass these around,” he said.

Noor looked at the screen. Her title slide glowed faintly enough to be readable. The rest of the presentation, the part she had spent three evenings perfecting, no longer looked like something she wanted anyone to see.

“If I use the prints, the order won't work,” she said.

“Then maybe the order can change.”

The first drops of rain tapped the metal roof as Noor walked to the front. She explained that the screen was difficult to see and held up the photograph of the ferry terminal instead. Before she could begin the paragraph she had memorized, an older man in the second row raised his hand.

“My father worked there,” he said. “The ticket window was on the other side before the renovation.”

Noor had never heard that detail. She asked him when the window had moved. A woman near the aisle disagreed with his date, and the two of them began comparing memories. Noor found the printed map and laid it across a table. Soon three audience members were pointing to different buildings, while another described the route children once took to school.

For a few minutes Noor worried that she had lost control of the presentation. Her notes contained no place for an argument about a ticket window. Then she noticed that people who had been waiting quietly for slides were leaning forward. She stopped trying to return to the original order. When someone mentioned a building, she found the closest photograph. When two memories conflicted, she wrote both versions in the margin of her notes instead of deciding which person was right.

The rain became heavier, drumming above them, but almost no one left.

Afterward, Noor packed the projector first. The unused slides still bothered her; she was not suddenly grateful that the screen had failed. On Monday she would probably revise them again. But she kept the printed photographs on top of the box instead of sliding them underneath the cables.

Mr. Han picked up the map covered with Noor's new notes. “Not exactly what you planned,” he said.

“No,” Noor replied. She looked at the two different dates written beside the ferry terminal. “But I think I know what the presentation was for now.”

On the bus home, she opened the slideshow on her laptop. Instead of deleting the first slide, she added a new one before it: QUESTIONS WE STILL HAVE. For the first time all week, she stopped arranging the rest.
